summary: A stone CCC-era tower on Wayah Bald in Nantahala NF, dedicated 1937, retired 1945, burned in 2016 and rebuilt with a new timber top; reopened 2018.

facts.design: Quarry-stone tower, 53 feet tall, topped by an oak roof; the top was rebuilt in timber after the 2016 fire
facts.status_note: The upper structure burned in the November 2016 Camp Branch Fire, leaving only the stone base; a new timber top was built and the tower reopened in 2018.

access.note: Closed to the public after the 2016 fire and reopened in 2018 per Wikipedia. No source confirms current climbing rules.

visit.trail_note: A few feet from the Appalachian Trail and the Bartram Trail

events.note: A 1936 newspaper planned a 43-foot stone tower to replace a 25-foot wooden tower; the Forest Service dates the wooden tower to about 1929
Built by the CCC; Wikipedia and the NHLR give 1937 while the Forest Service gives 1935 for the CCC work; dedicated on Labor Day and opened September 6, 1937
Retired from service per the Forest Service
Cab removed; per the NHLR the stone tower was then restored as a popular observation site
Restored and maintained by the Forest Service, per the Forest Service
Forest Service restored the north face in 2009 and 2010, per Wikipedia
Camp Branch Fire burned the upper structure, leaving only the stone base
Temporarily closed to the public after the fire
Reopened after a new timber top was built; the Forest Service also replaced the wooden roof

corrections.why: The NHLR and the Forest Service both give 53 feet (16.2 m) for the stone tower. The record's 7.6 m equals 25 feet, the height of the wooden tower the stone tower was meant to replace.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikipedia and the NHLR give 1937 for the CCC stone tower; the Forest Service gives 1935 for the CCC construction. The tower was dedicated and opened in September 1937, so we keep 1937 as the build year and report the 1935 claim in the story.
The Forest Service says the tower was retired from service in 1945; the NHLR says the cab was removed in 1947. Both dates are reported as separate events.
The NHLR gives 5,280 ft (1,609 m) and Wikipedia gives 5,385 ft for the area's highest point. We keep the NHLR figure already in the record.

notes_for_editor: The record's 7.6 m height was the earlier 25-foot wooden tower; corrected to 53 ft (16.2 m). The 1935 versus 1937 build date is unresolved; no NRHP nomination or Forest Service history was read. Eastern US Lookouts quotes a 1936 newspaper plan for a 43-foot stone tower, but the built height was 53 feet. The NHLR and Eastern US Lookouts spell the memorial name Bryne; the Forest Service and Eastern's 1939 quote use Byrne. Current climbing rules and hours were not found in any source. The 2016 fire is dated November 23, 2016 by Eastern US Lookouts only.
